body:
Here are some of my findings so far, as talked about [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113279#issuecomment-3628394818):

> 1. I've been able to reproduce this on macOS Tahoe, Linux (Fedora 42) and Windows 11.
> 1. Removing the added line to `gdscript_vm.cpp` makes no difference, so I guess that rules out [#113279](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113279).
> 1. Building with `TRACY_ON_DEMAND` did not help. It did however cause Tracy to sometimes immediately terminate the profiling session when connecting due to the same profiling zone having been exited multiple times, or something along those lines.
> 1. Having Tracy connected or not connected makes no difference, with or without `TRACY_ON_DEMAND`.
> 1. On Windows (even with 15-ish GB of memory to spare) the editor crashes at a `memcpy` in the Tracy code halfway through the resource importing, due to a `tracy_malloc` seemingly having returned a `nullptr`, while Tracy is trying to allocate more capacity for its `m_serialQueue` as part of `GodotProfileFree`. I assume this crashes because `tracy::FastVector` always doubles the memory on every grow, and the next doubling would exceed my 64 GB of total memory.
> 1. Looking at the calls to `tracy::FastVector<T>::AllocMore()`, I can confirm that it is indeed `tracy::Profiler::m_serialQueue` that grows so very big.
> 1. I figured it might be that Tracy only flushes this `m_serialQueue` every frame or something, and `ProgressDialog` (which is a potentially long-running modal dialog) does not have a `GodotProfileFrameMark` in its `_update_ui` method, but adding one made no difference, unfortunately.
> 1. Setting `GodotProfileAlloc` and `GodotProfileFree` to be no-ops **does** resolve the issue.
> 
> So it would seem that this is caused by Tracy's memory profiling somehow, either because we're failing to do something to flush this queue, or we're just doing so many allocations during resource importing that this sort of tracking scales poorly to bigger projects.
This was mitigated by #113807 which made memory profiling optional with a new `profiler_track_memory` SCons argument (defaults to False, so this bug isn't reproducible by default).
I've updated/reframed the issue to include the new `profiler_track_memory=yes` build option.

I was cleaning out my emails and this popped up so i did some quick research in the discord channel for Tracy and found this [conversation](https://discord.com/channels/585214693895962624/585214693895962630/785255359077154876) from 2020 which i will paste below(skipping all the inbetween).

---

> **TaintedHermit**:
> Hello all, I am currently in the process of integrating Tracy with one of our projects at work. Has anyone any idea if it has been integrated for consoles specially the Nintendo Switch?
> 
> I have been able to get the traces show up for switch after some work. But I am currently seeing a crash in rpmalloc after a while which is due to me running over virtual to physical mapping limit on the client side. The problem I am seeing is the call to _memory_unmap_os is never getting called due to which the memory allocation skyrockets.

> **wolfpld**:
> try using non-rpmalloc calls in TracyAlloc.hpp

> **TaintedHermit**:
> I switched to non-rpmalloc calls but I still run out of memory after a while. Does this mean I have lot of traces on in my application? Do I need to cut them down or profile for a shorter period of time? tracy_free is getting called only when I shut down the application not during profiling.

> **wolfpld**:
> this is by design
> tracy will use all the memory you have to store all recorder events
> you may want to use the on-demand mode, which will only capture events when there's a connection that can immediately handle them

> **TaintedHermit**:
> So basically Tracy grabs memory and only releases it until the application is closed.  Our initial thought was that it will buffer up what it can and than send it to the server, and than start over.
> Will do some runs with on-demand mode and try to focus on problematic areas.

> **benvanik**:
> (I too had thought if the connection was active the memory would be flushed - is that not the case?)

> **woldpld**:
> the event buffer memory is not freed
> things like strings, are
> note that this is the design decision of concurrentqueue
> and I think the problem here is determining when to free memory
> you don't want to be constantly allocating and deallocating buffers, or you'll get horrible memory fragmentation

> **benvanik**:
> ah - so it's really a peak usage issue (you're reclaiming and reusing the event buffers after the events have been flushed to the server, correct?)
> if so, then maybe an application-level "drain the tracy buffers" bit of logic may help - allow N frames to run and then pause until drained before continuing, etc
> and if you produce more events in a single frame (or span of time) then can be flushed you probably are generating too many events :)

> **TaintedHermit**:
> From the Tracy doc -
> > It should be noted, that if on-demand profiling is disabled (which is the default), then the recorded events
> > will be stored in the system memory until a server connection is made and the data can be uploaded.
> > Depending on the amount of the things profiled, the requirements for event storage can easily grow up to
> > a couple of gigabytes. Since this data is cleared after the initial connection is made, you won’t be able to
> > perform a second connection to a client, unless the on-demand mode is used.
> 
> It seems like the stored data is transferred to the server upon initial connection.

> **wolfpld**:
> > **benvanik**:
> > ah - so it's really a peak usage issue (you're reclaiming and reusing the event buffers after the events have been flushed to the server, correct?)
> 
> yes

---

That's the end of the conversation, I will try to find one about manually flushing to the server, and I hope this style of comment is OK.

This is a path I would look into

---

> lc:
> Tracy is creating a bunch of memory and then crashing for me

> zAhmed:
> Are you attaching the tracy profiler server to stream the data?

> lc:
> I was, it still did. Turned out apparently I was creating too many profiler regions in an 100% epoll loop with timeout set to 0. Changed it to 1ms and we're all good lol
